strengths: Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements of 1-9% over state-of-the-art baselines (LESS, TAGCOS) across multiple tasks, with TRIM sometimes exceeding full-data fine-tuning performance
Clear problem motivation: Well-articulated critique of sample-level selection methods (length bias, loss-centric bias) with principled token-level solution
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple task evaluations, out-of-domain testing (GSM8K), cross-model transferability, length bias analysis, and task-adaptive behavior demonstration
Significant computational efficiency: Forward-only design achieves O(fN) scoring cost vs O(3fNC) for gradient-based alternatives; practical speedup for large-scale coreset selection
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, complete pseudocode, public datasets/models, and thorough appendices enable reproduction

Strong out-of-domain performance: Selecting from general-purpose corpus for mathematical reasoning (8.8% improvement over LESS) demonstrates capture of structural rather than superficial task properties
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification for design choices: Why entropy for row saliency and average weights for column saliency? Equal hyperparameter weights (0.5/0.5) appear arbitrary without principled justification beyond ablations

Insufficient robustness analysis of target set dependence: Method critically depends on Tval quality and representativeness, but robustness to small, noisy, or biased validation sets is barely explored; no experiments with 2-3 examples or deliberately poor samples
Ad-hoc OOV handling: Fallback to nearest embedding neighbor with penalty λ is unprincipled; 1.4% performance gap between λ=1.0 and λ=0.5 is substantial but unexplored
Missing qualitative analysis: No examples of learned fingerprints, selected tokens, or interpretability analysis to validate whether TRIM captures meaningful task structure
Limited evaluation scope: Only 4 tasks (all multiple-choice or math); no generation tasks; largest model tested is 8B (scaling to 70B+ untested); budget exploration mostly at 5% coreset

Unvalidated attention-importance assumption: Paper assumes attention weights correlate with token importance but doesn't validate this or compare with alternative token importance measures (gradients, attribution methods)
Warmup dependency underexplored: 5% random warmup is critical but sensitivity to warmup composition not analyzed; unclear whether warmup quality matters more than target set quality
Statistical testing absent: Standard deviations reported but no significance tests; some baseline differences (e.g., 45.37% vs 44.21%) are small relative to variance

Limited novelty: Combines existing techniques (attention analysis + representation matching) without deep methodological innovation; applicability restricted to scenarios with target validation sets (excludes pretraining)
Asymptotic computational analysis only: Section 5 provides Big-O analysis but acknowledges not reporting actual wall-clock times; true speedup depends on implementation details and memory usage

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation clearly articulating limitations of sample-level methods (length bias, loss-centric bias) with compelling case for token-level approach
Strong and consistent empirical results outperforming LESS/TAGCOS by up to 9% across multiple benchmarks with proper error bars; exceeds full-data fine-tuning on some tasks with only 5% coreset
Genuine practical computational efficiency advantage with clear asymptotic analysis (O(fN) vs O(3fNC)); forward-only design avoids expensive backward passes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including cross-model transfer (Table 3), length bias analysis (Figure 3), task-adaptive selection patterns (Figure 4), and ablations (Table 8)
Clear presentation and well-structured writing with informative figures; two-stage pipeline is easy to follow; detailed pseudocode provided
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—straightforward combination of existing techniques (Abnar & Zuidema 2020 attention saliency, weighted averaging, cosine similarity) without significant innovation; appears primarily engineering-oriented

Weak theoretical foundation: assumes attention entropy correlates with token importance but provides no empirical validation comparing attention-based rankings to actual gradient norms; no evidence the method approximates token-wise gradients as claimed

Serious experimental fairness concerns: warmup phase confounds results; all methods do 5% warmup but TRIM uses only forward passes while baselines use backward passes; the random 5% subset could contain many high-quality examples; no ablation isolating selection quality from warmup strategy by having all methods score from identical checkpoint

Insufficient robustness analysis: method depends critically on 5-10 target examples but lacks sensitivity testing (biased validation sets, number of examples required); hyperparameter choices (wQ=wK=0.5, wμ=wm=0.5, λ penalty) justified only 'for simplicity'; ablations limited to single task (CommonsenseQA); OOV token backoff strategy is ad-hoc with no validation of frequency or impact

Missing validation of core claims about 'structural fidelity': Figure 4 shows task-adaptive selection but doesn't prove these patterns cause performance gains; no qualitative analysis of selected samples; no visualization of fingerprints or representation space; GSM8K full-data baseline (30.25%) suspiciously low, raising calibration concerns

Incomplete baseline comparisons: T-SHIRT (token-level selection) dismissed without empirical comparison; LADM and other recent token-centric methods mentioned but not experimentally evaluated; missing comparisons with simpler token-level alternatives

Statistical rigor issues: only 3 seeds without power analysis; improvements over LESS sometimes ~1-2% within noise margins; Table 3 oracle sometimes underperforms transfer (suspicious); no significance testing beyond standard deviations; Table 1 improvements not clearly significant

Technical clarity problems: entropy normalization (Eq. 2) unclear; fingerprint L2-normalization (Eq. 9) design choice lacks justification/ablation; coverage term κ(c) reintroduces length bias concerns but hidden in appendix; selective token scoring validated only theoretically, not empirically

strengths: Well-motivated token-level approach addressing clear limitations (length bias, loss-centric bias) of sample-level data selection methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks with consistent improvements (up to 9% on GSM8K) and particularly impressive out-of-domain results
Surprising and interesting cross-model transfer results (Table 3) showing 1B-selected coresets outperform oracle selections on larger models, suggesting learned patterns generalize
Practical efficiency with O(fN) forward-only scoring vs. O(3fNC) for gradient-based alternatives, enabling scalable selection over massive corpora
Strong empirical analysis including length bias mitigation (Figure 3), task-adaptive selection patterns (Figure 4), and thorough ablations (Table 8)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed pseudocode, hyperparameters, multiple seeds with standard deviations, and comprehensive appendices
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) and honest discussion of limitations and constraints
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution combines existing techniques (attention interpretation, representation matching, fingerprinting) in a fairly straightforward manner rather than introducing fundamentally new insights
Reliance on attention as a faithful importance signal is under-validated; no ablation comparing attention-based saliency to simpler baselines or exploring sensitivity to attention head quality

Target validation set dependency under-explored: critical questions unanswered about robustness to smaller target sets (<5 examples), noisy labels, or biased selections despite being central to the method
Warmup phase adds implicit cost (5% of data for training Mwarmup) not always highlighted; fairness concern whether this overhead equally impacts all compared methods
Improvements vary substantially across tasks (0.5% on HellaSwag, 1.2% on SocialIQA, 8.8% on GSM8K); some gains are marginal and significance testing not provided despite reporting standard deviations

Limited evaluation scope: only 1B-8B models (unclear scaling for larger LLMs), instruction tuning only (not pretraining), four target tasks, and no comparison to other token-centric methods (LADM, T-SHIRT)

Design choices appear ad-hoc (equal weights wQ=wK=0.5, wμ=wm=0.5, λ=1.0, last 6 layers) with insufficient justification beyond limited ablations; entropy-based saliency normalization (Eq. 2) is heuristic
TRIM-Transfer outperforming TRIM-Oracle (Table 3) is striking but inadequately explained—lacks investigation into why smaller models select better-generalizing coresets
Potential for amplifying target set biases into fingerprints and downstream selection; no discussion of fairness implications or mitigation strategies
Selective token scoring (response-only, prompt-only) mentioned as hyperparameter in Appendix B.1 but not explored experimentally despite potentially being significant for task-specific performance

strengths: Significant practical efficiency gains (8-10× speedup over LESS) with competitive accuracy on core benchmarks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: benchmarks, model scales/architectures, robustness studies, and extensive ablations
Clear demonstration of mitigating length bias through token-level scoring with empirical evidence (Figure 3)
Strong performance on challenging downstream tasks with low topical overlap (GSM8K: 29.52% vs 20.72% for LESS)
Cross-model transfer results demonstrate that token-level fingerprints capture model-agnostic structure generalizing to different architectures
Well-structured paper with clear presentation, detailed pseudocode, and thorough appendices including qualitative analysis
Practical versatility shown through targeted and in-domain selection variants
weaknesses: Core assumption that attention patterns proxy data importance lacks empirical validation; no direct comparison between attention-derived and gradient-derived token importance scores
Limited methodological novelty—straightforward application of standard techniques (row/column saliency, weighted averaging, cosine matching) without conceptual innovation
Improvements over LESS marginal in many settings with overlapping error bars (MMLU: 49.33±0.4 vs 49.23±0.3; performance worse on TRUTHFULQA)
Critical design choices lack justification: equal weighting of row/column saliency (no ablation), extreme sensitivity to NFF penalty λ (0.5→46%, 0.9→49%, suggesting brittleness), minimal IDF impact
Fingerprinting robustness concerns: token-class fingerprints from only 5-10 examples may not capture contextual variations; significant performance degradation with noisy targets (100% noise→27.29%)
Insufficient comparison with related attention-based methods; LADM and T-SHIRT mentioned but not empirically compared
Limited theoretical understanding of when method succeeds/fails; no formal characterization of conditions where attention-based selection should work
Evaluation limited to instruction-tuning and knowledge/reasoning tasks; generalization to other adaptation scenarios and very large models (70B+) unclear
Some supporting results in appendices suggest design space exploration was limited and hyperparameter choices (wQ, wK, wµ, wm) may be task-dependent

strengths: Computational efficiency: Forward-only design achieves 4.4 hours vs 35+ hours for gradient-based methods, providing genuine practical speedup for the one-time selection stage

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA, GSM8K), cross-model transfer studies, robustness tests (noisy/small validation sets), and detailed ablations demonstrate thorough investigation
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written with effective Figure 1 overview, pseudocode (Algorithms 1-3), detailed hyperparameters, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Length bias mitigation: Concrete evidence (Figure 3) that TRIM selects longer sequences (446 tokens) than LESS (323), providing more complex reasoning examples
Addresses real limitations of prior work: Identifies legitimate issues with sample-level scoring (length bias, loss-centric bias) and proposes token-level alternative
weaknesses: Marginal and statistically insignificant improvements: On main benchmarks at 5% budget—MMLU 49.33 vs LESS 49.23 (0.1 pt), BBH 39.73 vs 39.45 (0.28 pt), TyDiQA 56.62 vs 56.13 (0.49 pt)—all differences fall within standard deviations (~0.3-0.4). No significance testing provided despite overlapping confidence intervals. Only GSM8K shows substantial gains (29.52 vs 20.72), but this is a single outlier task

Weak theoretical foundation: The core assumption that attention-based saliency predicts data importance is asserted but never validated. No evidence linking attention patterns (row/column saliency) to downstream learning outcomes. The connection between 'tokens that attend sharply' and 'examples that teach useful structures' is assumed without causal analysis

Unexplained collapse of advantage on domain-aligned data: In Section 4.5 (in-domain MATHINSTRUCT), TRIM achieves 52.23% on GSM8K vs LESS 52.10%—essentially tied. This directly contradicts the 'structural fidelity' narrative used to explain GSM8K superiority. If TRIM truly captures mathematical reasoning structure better, why does advantage vanish with domain-aligned candidates?

Ad-hoc design choices lacking principled justification: (1) Inconsistent normalization schemes (entropy for row saliency, min-max for column) without ablation; (2) Pooling strategy combines mean/max with fixed 0.5/0.5 weights—ablation (Table 10) shows all variants within 1.2 points, suggesting choice is inconsequential; (3) NFF penalty λ=0.9 appears tuned to results; (4) IDF reweighting has negligible impact (Table 11: 49.43 vs 49.31); (5) Layer count barely matters (Table 9: 49.33 vs 49.43 for 6 vs 12 layers)

Limited novelty: Token-centric selection (T-SHIRT, LADM), attention-based saliency analysis, and fingerprinting via averaging are all established techniques. The contribution combines existing components without significant methodological innovation

Incomplete analysis of length bias claim: Section 4.4 demonstrates TRIM selects longer sequences but never validates this improves performance or that length bias mitigation correlates with better downstream results. Could be a confound of the scoring mechanism rather than principled mitigation

Weak cross-model transfer: TRIM-Transfer underperforms TRIM-Oracle on LLAMA-2-13B (BBH: 49.83 vs 50.02) and significantly on Mistral-7B (MMLU: 60.40 vs 61.72), suggesting coresets are model-specific and undermining the claimed efficiency advantage of selecting once

Unsubstantiated claims in abstract: Abstract claims 'up to 9% improvements' and 'surpass full-data fine-tuning'—the 9% only appears on GSM8K (a specialized domain-mismatch setting), and full-data surpassing occurs on only 1-2 tasks. Main benchmark improvements are ~0.3 points

Lack of statistical rigor: No significance tests (t-tests, confidence intervals) despite clear overlapping standard deviations. Three random seeds is minimal. Results described as 'improvements' without statistical validation

Insufficient explanation of GSM8K outlier: The paper asserts that token-level fingerprints capture 'stepwise logic, numerical manipulation' but provides no qualitative analysis of which examples are selected, what patterns TRIM identifies, or why this advantage vanishes on domain-aligned pools
Limited experimental scope: Primarily evaluated on instruction tuning with Llama-2-7B. Only 4 main benchmarks. Unknown generalization to other domains beyond instruction tuning

Design choices appear tuned to results: Many hyperparameters (NFF penalty, coverage weight, layer count) show sensitivity profiles where the chosen value is not clearly optimal, suggesting possible overfitting to validation benchmarks

strengths: Significant practical computational speedup: 8x faster than LESS (4.4 vs 35.76 hours) with asymptotically better complexity O(fN) vs O(3fNC), directly addressing real computational constraints in instruction tuning

Strong empirical results on challenging downstream tasks: 29.52% on GSM8K vs 20.72% for LESS at 5% budget (+8.8%), demonstrating that token-level signals capture task structure better than sample-level signals

Addresses well-identified systematic biases: inherently mitigates length bias (446 vs 323 token average) and loss-centric bias through token-level attention-based scoring rather than aggregated signals

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple settings (budgeted accuracy, cross-scale/architecture transfer, in-domain selection), thorough ablations (Tables 9-13), robustness testing (Section J), and out-of-task evaluation (Table 14) with 3 seeds and standard deviations

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear methodology with helpful visualizations (Figure 1), complete pseudocode (Appendix B), detailed hyperparameters (Table 8), and extensive supplementary material (27+ pages)

Practical applicability and flexibility: works with minimal target examples (5-10), transfers across model scales/architectures, supports in-domain selection, and scales to massive corpora (270k examples)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for design choices: claims that low entropy attention indicates importance are intuitive but lack rigor; no theoretical analysis of why attention-derived saliency should correlate with influence; missing ablation comparing to simpler baselines like direct hidden state similarity

Empirically-motivated rather than principled design: equal weights wQ=wK=0.5 justified only as 'simplicity'; pooling weights (0.5·MEAN+0.5·MAX+0.05·COVERAGE) appear hand-tuned; IDF reweighting actually hurts performance (Table 11: 49.43→49.31) yet remains in defaults

Statistical significance concerns on standard benchmarks: MMLU improvements (49.33±0.4 vs 49.23±0.3 for LESS) likely overlap; BBH similar (39.73±0.89 vs 39.45±0.2); only GSM8K shows clearly significant gains, making main claims partially unsupported

Missing comparisons with related token-level methods: no direct comparison to QCS (Chen et al., 2025b), LADM (Chen et al., 2025a), or T-SHIRT (Fu et al., 2025) despite these being most relevant; dismissal of QCS/T-SHIRT as 'computationally heavy' lacks empirical support

Mechanism of improvement incompletely understood: why does matching token fingerprints select better data? 'Structural fidelity' argument (Section 4.2) remains intuitive without rigorous analysis; limited qualitative analysis of what examples TRIM selects vs alternatives; connection between target-set attention patterns and broader coreset utility is assumed not validated

Target validation set requirements not fully explored: method requires hand-crafted Tval; robustness testing only covers size (5-100 examples, Table 15) and noisy answers (Table 16), not domain shift or quality variations; claim of 'as few as 5-10' samples misleading given clear improvement trajectory through 20 examples

Mixed transfer results weaken generalization claims: LLAMA-2-13B shows TRIM-Transfer underperforming oracle on BBH (49.83 vs 50.02) and other tasks; MISTRAL-7B misses oracle on MMLU (60.43 vs 61.72); explanations for variable transfer success are incomplete

In-domain selection feels secondary: results match rather than beat baselines (52.23 vs 52.10/52.45, Table 4); motivation and novelty unclear; uses different Tval construction (Tval⊂S) than main method, blurring contribution boundaries
